items.summary: A number without a unit is not a measurement, and a formula whose two sides do not match in units is not a formula. After reading this you can name the seven base units, write a measurement the way a drawing expects it, check a formula with dimensional analysis, and explain why a converted number can be right in arithmetic and wrong in meaning.
items.title: Units, Dimensions and Dimensional Analysis

items.summary: An airport looks like one big building until you try to find a gate in it. After reading this you can read the signs, follow the process in the right order, transfer between flights without panic, and ask the right question when the plan breaks.
items.title: Navigating an Airport Without Getting Lost

items.summary: A menu in a language you do not read is a short problem with a known solution. After reading this you can read any menu, order exactly what you want, explain a dietary need, pay the right amount and tip in the local way.
items.title: Ordering Food in a Foreign Country

items.summary: Losing a passport is a bureaucratic problem, not a disaster, but only if you act in the right order. After reading this you can report the loss correctly, get the right documents from the right office, and travel home while you wait.
items.title: What to Do When You Lose Your Passport

items.summary: Professional email is a written register with its own rules: a subject line that gets opened, a structure the reader can scan, and a tone that survives being read without your voice. After reading this you can write a clear request, a careful apology, a firm refusal and a follow-up, and you will know the words each of them needs.
items.title: Writing Professional Emails in English

items.summary: An interview introduction is not a biography. It is a short, structured answer that tells the interviewer who you are, why you are relevant and what you want next. After reading this you can prepare a 60-second introduction, describe your experience with evidence, ask questions that show judgement, and close the interview and follow up in a way that is remembered.
items.title: How to Introduce Yourself in a Job Interview

items.summary: A request for a raise is a business case, not a favour. It works when you arrive with evidence, a number and a calm plan. After reading this you will know when to ask, how to build the evidence, how to say the sentence out loud, and what to do in the week after you hear no.
items.title: How to Ask for a Raise Politely

items.summary: Persuasion is ordinary in a negotiation; the dark part is using it to hide the real price, the real stock or the real deadline. After reading this you can name nine techniques, say what the honest version of the same request is, and prepare the two things that protect you: your alternative and your walk-away price.
items.title: Dark Psychology in Business and Negotiation

items.summary: An average difference between two groups says where the centres of two clouds sit, not where any one person stands. After reading this you can name the five parts of emotional maturity, say what a claim about men and women can and cannot tell you about one person, read a group claim without turning it into a rule, and hold a conversation about it without the argument becoming a fight.
items.title: Gender Differences in Emotional Maturity

items.summary: Mate selection is the process of choosing a partner, and it has its own vocabulary. After reading this you can separate attraction, preference and decision, describe how people actually choose, read the direction and the size of an age gap, and run a short check on the preferences you say you hold.
items.title: Mate Selection and Age Preferences

items.summary: Attachment styles describe the promises a person brings to a partner, the way they read availability, and what they do when a partner is unavailable. After reading this you can name the four styles, describe what each one looks for and fears, recognise the signals that switch your own pattern on, and say what you need in words your partner can act on.
items.title: Attachment Styles in Romantic Relationships

items.summary: Competence shaming is a way of gaining standing by lowering somebody else's competence, and the difference from honest criticism is the aim, not the words. After reading this you can name the four moves of the attack, tell honest criticism from a status attack, answer one without escalating it, and notice when you are doing it yourself.
items.title: Competence Shaming and Status Manipulation

items.summary: An argument can be lost without a single false fact. When the ground moves — to the person, to the feeling, to a standard that changes after the facts arrive — the claim is never tested. After reading this you can name the nine moves, spot them in a live exchange, answer each one with one sentence, and keep your own argument clean when you are being pushed.
items.title: Psychological Manipulation in Arguments

items.summary: Gaslighting is the rewriting of a shared account until the person who was there doubts their own memory. After reading this you can tell a deliberate attack apart from an ordinary disagreement and an honest mistake, name the three moves of DARVO, recognise the pattern in plain language at work and at home, and answer it with sentences you can reuse.
items.title: Gaslighting and DARVO: Manipulating Perception and Turning the Blame Around

items.summary: Long-term singleness has a vocabulary of its own, and much of the trouble around it comes from using the wrong word. After reading this you can tell the state of being single from the story a person tells about it, name the words that describe it precisely, recognise the pressure underneath it, and answer the questions other people ask without apologising for the answer.
items.title: The Psychology of Long-Term Singleness

items.summary: The dating market is a metaphor, not a law, and hypergamy is a hypothesis that people still argue about. After reading this you can explain what the metaphor describes and what it assumes, name the words the subject uses, state what the hypothesis predicts and what it cannot explain, compare it with the other answers for the same pattern, and use the vocabulary without turning people into a ranking.
items.title: The Dating Market and the Hypergamy Hypothesis

items.summary: Emotions do not decide what you say next, and relationships run on rules nobody writes down. After reading this you can tell the difference between regulating a feeling and hiding it, describe what a partner sees when a feeling is suppressed, reappraised or rehearsed, name the expectations under a conflict, and use short sentences to ask for a pause, state a need and agree a repair.
items.title: Emotional Regulation and Relationship Expectations

items.summary: Power is the ability to make things happen; authority is power the other side accepts. After reading this you can tell the two apart, name the five bases on which authority is claimed, test whether a decision can be questioned, and raise an objection in a meeting, in a review or in writing without turning the difference into insubordination.
items.title: Power Dynamics and Authority Manipulation

items.summary: A gender role is a rule about what a category of people is expected to do. After reading this you can tell a role from a stereotype, name who enforces the rule around you, see how the cost of breaking it falls on one person, and negotiate a division of work at home or at work before the next crisis decides it for you.
items.title: Gender Roles and Social Expectations

items.summary: The biological clock is a phrase, not a device, and it mixes a real biological change with a social deadline. After reading this you can tell fertility, fecundity and the ovarian reserve apart, say what menopause and perimenopause name, explain where reproductive urgency and timeline pressure come from, and hold a conversation about timing without panic.
items.title: The Biological Clock and Reproductive Psychology

items.summary: Loneliness is a feeling, and being alone is a fact, and the two are easily confused. After reading this you can tell loneliness, isolation, alienation and solitude apart, explain why a standard rises and what a closed door costs, describe commitment as a series of small decisions, and say what you want from a relationship in sentences you can use.
items.title: Loneliness, Selectivity and Commitment

items.summary: Marriage timing is not one decision but a set of forces: work, money, study, family, law and the people around you. After reading this you can name the forces that push a date earlier or later, use the vocabulary of timing accurately, tell the peer effect from the family effect, and run a short procedure that separates the practical questions from the pressure.
items.title: The Psychology of Marriage Timing
